title: Huawei's Ascend chose the hardest road: not compatible with Nvidia
dek: For three or four decades Chinese IT has been a follower. Ascend is Huawei's first product that doesn't solve a chokehold problem but instead walks into uncharted territory, starting at the same time as Nvidia. Xu Zhijun said: anything you do as a follower gets harder and harder the longer you do it.
why: The first half is about how the book was written, with low information density; from the two key decisions at Ascend's founding, Fang Xingdong gives a lot of frontline detail and judgment that only exists in the book.
who: Founders, investors and engineers watching domestic compute, the semiconductor supply chain and AI infrastructure, especially those who want to understand the difference between Ascend's and Nvidia's routes.
skip: The first ~13 minutes cover the origin and interview process of the six books, with little bearing on investment judgment.

points.h: Ascend's harshest decision was not being compatible with Nvidia
points.body: At Ascend's founding there were two choices. The first was whether AI chips should be specialized or general-purpose; Liao Heng, as chief scientist, judged that AI should be a general-purpose product, and the architecture choice has been proven right today. The second was harder: whether to be compatible with Nvidia. Many domestic chips chose compatibility, with the benefit that Nvidia's existing ecosystem and tools could all be shared. But Xu Zhijun was firm from the start that they had to take a different path. Fang Xingdong believes this choice was extremely bold at the time, and that it faced enormous challenges many times along the way — because the entire Chinese IT industry has been a follower industry for three or four decades, and had never developed based on its own root technology.

points.h: Anything you do as a follower gets harder and harder
points.body: Fang Xingdong recalls having dinner with Xu Zhijun three years ago, when Xu half muttered to himself: Huawei has done this for so many years, and the discovery is that anything you do as a follower always gets harder and harder the longer you do it. There are two kinds of following: in standardized products, Chinese companies can always close the gap and even overtake, but by the time they overtake, there is no profit left in the industry — 2G to 5G, PCs, phones all went this way; in non-standardized areas, such as competing with Cisco in routers for so many years, the gap has not closed. In Xu Zhijun's eyes, what Huawei did in the past was also following. So Ascend is special among the six products: the other five solve chokeholds and address survival first, while Ascend was not choked in 2019 — it is a fully proactive compute product.

points.h: With process choked off, only system innovation can make it back
points.body: Industry chips gain roughly 20% or more performance each generation, mainly from the increase in transistor count driven by advanced process improvements. Huawei lost this premise and can only gain performance through system innovation and breakthroughs — stacked compute, interconnect, higher integration. Fang Xingdong explains with a car metaphor: before, you just had to make the engine stronger and stronger; now the engine is constrained and can no longer be enlarged, so you can only make the car run well through architecture, weight reduction, heat dissipation and other factors. Nvidia's solution is to keep working on the engine, because TSMC can still manufacture it. In the interview Liao Heng uses the metaphor of an 18-story pagoda: many companies are good at only one layer because of the great division of labor, while Huawei is forced to do manufacturing, ecosystem and chip design all at once.

points.h: Huawei has to pull the domestic supply chain up with it
points.body: Previously Huawei did design, relied on the global supply chain, had TSMC manufacture, could choose the best international partners for other components, directly buy American products and assemble them, sell at a good price with brand premium and decent profit. Now it cannot cooperate with foreign partners, TSMC cannot process for it, and domestic processes are still lacking in every respect, so Huawei has no choice but to support and drive the domestic supply chain — only then does it have a way to survive and get products manufactured. So the challenge of the past seven years is not just improving its own capabilities but also driving the entire supply chain — without driving it, independent autonomy is impossible. Manufacturing is not Huawei's main business, but it has to help companies like SMIC and Yangtze Memory keep advancing process, yield and quality.

points.h: Ascend's significance is not that Huawei survived, but that the industry has an engine
points.body: In the past, Huawei's product launches and iterations were still based on American root technology and industrial ecosystem, and the high-value components of a phone were basically foreign. Now Huawei's phones, including Ascend, drive almost 100% domestic supply chains. Fang Xingdong believes the greatest significance of the Tao Dinglv is not that Huawei itself can survive and be autonomous, but that China's entire semiconductor industry and entire IT industry have their own engine, which never existed before. Huawei's rapid development represents the rapid development of the entire industrial ecosystem. He also points out that the market, reading reports, news or public opinion, has not yet realized that we are at this inflection point — mention Nvidia and people think it is formidable, mention Huawei and they say it is policy that makes everyone use it.

points.h: It is not a question of difficulty, but of cognition and resolve
points.body: Fang Xingdong believes doing communications versus doing IT is essentially not a question of difficulty but of cognition and resolve — whether you dare to do it. The most typical example is the Gauss database: among these six products Ascend stood out, and the least conspicuous is probably Gauss, but the database is a half-century-old industry with a relatively stable market, and being choked on it would be deadly. At the time Huawei wanted to acquire or support domestic vendors, but after research found none of them were up to it — domestic companies could only grow in the cracks of American giants, small in scale, weak in R&D, weak in product innovation. So Huawei decided to do it itself, benchmarking Oracle, investing 1 billion, 2 billion, 3 billion yuan a year starting in 2011 and 2012, without knowing whether there would be any output in the future.

points.h: The future is two centers, not one replacing the other
points.body: Fang Xingdong judges that global high tech moving from a single system centered on the US to two centers is the general trend; politics will not allow a continued single center — the US will not allow it, and China will not allow it either. He believes a single center is itself abnormal, and only two centers can create competition — only with two systems does every consumer, every company, every country, no matter how big or small, have a choice, and not be choked into a forced either-or. So the mission of Huawei's six products is to go from second choice to better choice; the relationship with Nvidia is not simple substitution but each having strengths, complementing advantages, and co-opetition. He admits the American system is currently stronger, with its advantage mainly in advanced manufacturing, and that Huawei, under process constraints, uses the Tao Dinglv to avoid being left behind; once advanced process is also broken through, it can pursue both at once.

points.h: The tech war won in the short term, at a greater long-term cost
points.body: Fang Xingdong believes the US did indeed suppress Huawei through the tech war, but cannot solve the problem in the long term. He reasons: without the national confrontation of 2017 and 2018, Huawei might be at least one-third of Nvidia, one-third of Apple, and possibly China's largest company by market cap; in 2019 Huawei had already surpassed Apple, and its global shipments briefly exceeded Samsung's for one quarter. Nvidia today is dominant alone; if it had been running neck and neck with Huawei in AI chips from the start, it could not be in this position today. He judges that once the party being attacked builds a self-cycle that does not rely on the outside, and the other side cannot eliminate it even under the harshest conditions, it will be even harder to eliminate later — it will only grow stronger, turning from one monopoly into two competitors.

quotes.text: He said Huawei has done this for so many years, and the discovery is that anything you do as a follower always gets harder and harder the longer you do it.
I have been in this industry for 30 years, and I feel that many of my past understandings can all be reset to zero.
Without the tech war, Huawei is an excellent company, but it might not, would not become a great company; but with the tech war, it will certainly become a great company.

So the few hurdles Huawei faces now are actually about technology, but what it drives is the improvement of China's entire industry, the entire supply chain — yet many things it has to do itself first, because if it doesn't do them, no one else can.
Once the party being attacked, whether Huawei or China, builds a self-cycle, a self-cycle that does not rely on the outside, frankly speaking it becomes a long-term competitor.
